title: An Eighty-Year Nuclear Nightmare: The U.S., Japan, and Korea
author: Brad Wolf
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/hiroshima-
forum-680x350.jpeg)

Second International Hiroshima Forum.

On the right corner of my desk, next to my laptop and always in eyeshot, sits
a metal model of an atom bomb I assembled from a kit, a model of “[Little
Boy,”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Boy) the bomb the U.S. dropped on
Hiroshima. The model is made from aluminum alloy parts and is a 1/12th scale
of the original atom bomb, about nine inches long. The ad for the bomb
contained a video with dramatic music showing the model spinning through the
air as it falls toward its imagined target.

“Perfect for collectors,” the ad boasted. “A must-have for history
enthusiasts. Very enjoyable assembly process.”

Toward the bottom of the ad, perhaps as an afterthought, perhaps recognizing
the implications of marketing such a murderous model, was the following: “By
assembling this model, you can understand the history and moral issues of
nuclear weapons and trigger thoughts about the future of the world.”

The kit came with a tiny screwdriver, two dozen tiny screws, a sanding rod,
glue, and decals. The aluminum alloy parts were in molded plates. The model
even had a metal cart to assemble that the bomb sits on so it can be pulled
around your desk, pretending you’re getting ready to load it onto the [Enola
Gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enola_Gay), extinguish a city in a flash.

On the morning of August 6, 1945, the real “Little Boy” exploded with a flash
2,000 feet above the city of [Hiroshima, which sits on the Ota River delta on
Hiroshima Bay](https://japangeography.github.io/japan-geography/hiroshima-
geography/). The Ota River has six channels splitting Hiroshima into islets.
[Bomb victims](https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/survivors-hiroshima-
and-nagasaki/) staggered toward these channels to throw themselves into the
water hoping to extinguish their [burning
bodies](https://www.asahi.com/hibakusha/english/hiroshima/h00-00068-4e.html?msockid=2fdb9727bf1969d416db8111be456814).
The channels became so clogged with bodies that others couldn’t squeeze in.
Some people, closer to the hypocenter, were vaporized, reduced to shadows
seared into stone. Temperatures on the ground reached [4,000
degrees](https://min.news/en/military/a7bd4378b8b084ca1f8c485df07dedae.html#google_vignette).

As we once again approach that fateful day of August 6th, it is important to
recognize that not just the U.S. and Japan are intertwined in a nuclear
nightmare that has lasted over eighty years, but also [70,000
Koreans](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cp8zlwd3e42o) who were exposed to
the two atomic bombs incinerating Hiroshima and Nagasaki, people forcibly
removed from their homeland by the Japanese and sent to work in these cities.
Japan [colonized Korea in
1910](https://dh.scu.edu/exhibits/exhibits/show/korean-comfort-women--
history-/history) and for decades used Koreans as they saw fit, from [Comfort
Women](https://dh.scu.edu/exhibits/exhibits/show/korean-comfort-women--
history-/history) to slave labor. The Koreans then became atomic bomb victims,
despite their country not being at war with the United States. They are among
the unintended victims, the forgotten victims.

This November in Seoul, South Korea, the surviving Korean bomb victims will
testify at a [People’s Tribunal](http://abombtribunal.org/) holding the U.S.
accountable for war crimes. Lawyers from around the world have been preparing
legal briefs and will argue the case. The U.S. government is invited to appear
as the defendant at the Tribunal. The Republic of South Korea has also been
asked to appear as a witness.

Once let loose, an atomic bomb keeps on killing, generation after generation,
the cancers passed down to those not even born when the bombs first exploded.
The Korean atomic bomb victims, as well as the Japanese, have horrific stories
testifying to this. Children of the bomb. Atomic maladies. The bomb wages war
against the future.

The second atomic bomb that was dropped on August 9th incinerating another
Japanese city had a different nickname. That bomb had an even bigger belly and
used plutonium rather than uranium. They called it [“Fat
Man.”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Fat-Man) The same ad for the model of
the “Little Boy” atom bomb had a second ad inducing you to buy “Fat Man.” It
is another 1/12th scale model of the original, this one weighing 6.2 pounds
when completed. I declined the offer to buy and build it. One was repellent
enough.

The [U.S.](https://straitsresearch.com/statistic/countries-with-most-nuclear-
weapons) currently has 5,277 nuclear warheads.
[Russia](https://straitsresearch.com/statistic/countries-with-most-nuclear-
weapons) has 5,4490. [China](https://straitsresearch.com/statistic/countries-
with-most-nuclear-weapons), approximately 600. [France and the
U.K](https://straitsresearch.com/statistic/countries-with-most-nuclear-
weapons) have about 250 each and
[Israel](https://straitsresearch.com/statistic/countries-with-most-nuclear-
weapons) has about 90. [India, Pakistan, and North
Korea](https://straitsresearch.com/statistic/countries-with-most-nuclear-
weapons) bring up the rear with a few nukes each. In total there are over
[12,300 nuclear warheads](https://straitsresearch.com/statistic/countries-
with-most-nuclear-weapons) spanning the globe. The Korean atomic bomb victims
stand as ready reminders of what happens when these things are unleashed.
